facts: VENDOR ADVISORY (primary, retrieved from Wayback snapshot of opera.com): Opera KB 992, 'Advisory: Frameset issue allows execution of arbitrary code', Severity: Critical. Exact text: 'Framesets allow web pages to hold other pages inside them. Certain frameset constructs are not handled correctly when the page is unloaded, causing a memory corruption. To inject code, additional techniques will have to be employed.' Opera's response: 'Opera Software has released Opera 11.11, where this issue has been fixed.' Credits: 'an anonymous contributor working with the SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure program' (= Jose A. Vazquez / spa-s3c, SPAS3C-SV-004, SSD-1010101). File: /tmp/opera_kb992.html

FIX (primary): Opera 11.11 changelog (May 18, 2011, Wayback): 'Fixed an issue with framesets that could allow execution of arbitrary code, as reported by an anonymous contributor working with the SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure program; see our advisory.' The same 11.11 release also fixed crash issues CVE-2011-2629..2633 (pop-up reload, column-count CSS, Silverlight destruction, CRL handling). Gentoo bug 367837 marks the fix ebuild as opera-11.10.2109 (the Linux build number of the 11.11 release). File: /tmp/opera_1111.html

AFFECTED BAND (primary): NVD CPE for CVE-2011-2628: cpe opera:opera_browser:* with versionEndIncluding 11.10, enumerating 5.0 through 11.10 beta. NVD description: 'Opera before 11.11 does not properly implement FRAMESET elements, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via vectors related to page unload.' CVSS v2 10.0, CWE-20 per NVD. Tenable plugin 54587: 'Opera < 11.11 Multiple Vulnerabilities' (patched 2011-05-18). BID 47906 exists but securityfocus.com was not retrievable (bot-blocked).

RESEARCHER BAND (primary, spa-s3c blog PART-I, May 27, 2011, Spanish): 'La vulnerabilidad afecta a Opera v10.xx y Opera v11.xx (<11.11)'. He tested the original exploit 'desde v10.00 hasta v11.10 y todos consiguieron RCE al menos una vez' (every tested version 10.00-11.10 achieved RCE at least once; reliable on 10.61/10.62, degrading toward DoS in later versions). He rebuilt the exploit against v11.10 on Windows XP SP3 with DEP enabled (/nx=alwayson) achieving 80-90% reliable execution. Also tested successfully on Mac OS X Snow Leopard and Ubuntu Linux. URL: https://spa-s3c.blogspot.com/2011/05/spas3c-sv-004opera-browser-1111.html (file /tmp/spas3c.html)

CROSS-PRODUCT EVIDENCE (primary, same blog): the vulnerability 'se dispara con exito en Opera Mobile v11.x y Opera Mobile v10.x' - it fires on Opera Mobile (separate product line sharing the Presto core), tested by ARM debugging on a Nokia N8 / Symbian^3 with Carbide.c++/IDA: the Program Counter mostly loaded low values (0x134, 0x130 - commonly unexploitable) but sometimes crashed at heap/stack regions (0x005xxxxx, 0x006xxxxx), so ARM exploitation was 'not ruled out'. Also fired in the Windows Mobile emulator. Blog update: 'SecuriTeam reconoce haber notificado el tema movil a los desarrolladores de Opera que descartan tener un update cercano' - Opera acknowledged the mobile issue but ruled out a near-term mobile update.

DESKTOP-PRESTO MAPPING (primary sources): Opera 11.10 changelog states verbatim: 'Opera 11.10 uses the new Opera Presto 2.8 rendering engine... Opera/9.80 (Windows NT 5.1; U; en) Presto/2.8.131 Version/11.10' (file /tmp/opw_1110.html). Wikipedia Presto table: Presto 2.7.62 = Opera 11.0 (Kjevik); 2.8.131 (Barracuda) = Opera 11.1x; 2.9.168 (Swordfish) = Opera 11.5; 2.10.229 (Tunny) = Opera 11.6; 2.6.30 = Opera 10.6. CONSEQUENCE: the desktop Opera 11.10/11.11 line ran Presto 2.8.131, and the ONLY desktop releases on the Presto 2.7 line were Opera 11.00/11.01 (Presto 2.7.62). NOTE: this corrects the session context's claim that 'Presto 2.7.62 shipped in Opera 11.11' - 2.7.62 shipped in 11.00/11.01; 11.11 shipped 2.8.131.

PRESTO 2.7.61 IS NOT A DESKTOP VERSION: no desktop Opera release ever shipped Presto 2.7.61 (the 2.7 desktop line is 2.7.62 only, in 11.00/11.01). 2.7.61 is therefore an Opera Devices SDK branch build of the Presto 2.7 core - i.e., the core generation of desktop Opera 11.00 (Kjevik, released Dec 2010), taken at a build point one below the desktop final. Sony's own fleet confirms the pattern: the 2012 HX855 runs Presto/2.10.250 (desktop 11.60 line = 2.10.229, an SDK build number off the desktop shipping number) per /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/research/webfindings.md, which also records the EX725 UA: 'Opera/9.80 (Linux mips; U; HbbTV/1.1.1 (; Sony; KDL40EX725; PKG4.021EUA...) Presto/2.7.61'.

IS 2.7.61 IN THE 2628 BAND - CERTAIN PART: the band is 'all Opera through 11.10', which in core terms spans Presto 2.2.x (Opera 10.00, tested by the author) through 2.8.131 (Opera 11.10). Presto 2.7.61 is numerically inside that core range; the affected code (frameset constructs mishandled at page unload) is core layout-engine code, not platform integration code; and the researcher demonstrated the bug fires not only across all desktop versions 10.00-11.10 but also on Opera Mobile builds of the same core generation (Mobile 11.0 shipped Presto 2.7.62 per Wikipedia) - i.e., the vulnerable path is present in non-desktop builds of the 2.7 core. INFERRED PART: the EX725's 2.7.61 Devices SDK build contains the vulnerable frameset-unload code path. Not certain because (a) no advisory or test covers an Opera Devices SDK build; (b) SDK builds are separately branched and could carry backported or divergent core code; (c) even on desktop, exploit reliability varied (DoS-only on several versions); (d) MIPS exploitability specifically was never tested (author tested x86 and partially ARM; on ARM the PC often loaded low, mostly-unexploitable values).

DEVICES LINE STAYED UNFIXED: Opera's only fix for CVE-2011-2628 is the desktop 11.11 release (Presto 2.8.131 maintenance of Barracuda). Per the SecuriTeam note quoted on the blog, Opera ruled out a near-term mobile update for this issue; no Opera Devices SDK security advisory for 2628 exists (none found in searching). A 2011-shipping TV SDK frozen on the 2.7 core therefore almost certainly never received this fix.

OTHER-ERA PRESTO CVE BANDS (all from NVD API records; all bands are desktop-scoped 'before X' with boilerplate CPE enumeration back to Opera 5.0, so the effective code-level range is unknown - only the fixed version and the bug's subsystem are certain): CVE-2012-3561 - Opera 'does not properly allocate memory for URL strings', memory corruption/possible code execution via crafted string; before 11.64 (CPE versionEndIncluding 11.62), fixed 11.64, KB 1016, CVSS v2 10.0. CVE-2012-6465 - execute arbitrary code or crash via malformed SVG image; before 12.10, fixed 12.10, KB 1033. CVE-2012-6468 - heap-based buffer overflow via a long HTTP response; before 12.11 (CPE <=12.10), fixed 12.11, KB 1036, BID 56594. CVE-2012-6470 - 'does not properly allocate memory for GIF images', memory overwrite/RCE/DoS via malformed image; before 12.12 (CPE <=12.11), fixed 12.12, KB 1038. CVE-2013-1637 - execute arbitrary code via vectors involving DOM events; before 12.13 (CPE <=12.12), fixed 12.13, KB 1042. CVE-2013-1638 - execute arbitrary code via crafted clipPaths in an SVG document; before 12.13, fixed 12.13, KB 1043.

BAND-COVERAGE VERDICT FOR 2.7.61 (inference ladder): (a) CVE-2012-1003 DEFINITIVELY DOES NOT COVER 2.7.61 despite its nominal '<= 11.60' band: it is integer overflow in Khronos typed arrays (Int32Array/Float32Array/Float64Array/Uint32Array/Int16Array/ArrayBuffer), and typed arrays were introduced only in Opera 11.60 (changelog-verified: 'Implemented support for Khronos Typed Arrays... XMLHttpRequest Level 2 support for receiving ArrayBuffers', file /tmp/opw_1160.html); the Presto 2.7 core predates them, so the vulnerable code path does not exist in 2.7.61. The vendor also called it 'a stability issue, not a security issue'. (b) For 2012-3561/6465/6468/6470 and 2013-1637/1638, every nominal band ('before 11.64' through 'before 12.13') includes Opera 11.00 and hence nominally a 2.7.61 core, and each bug's subsystem (URL string allocation, SVG parsing, HTTP response handling, GIF decoding, DOM events, SVG clipPath) existed in the Presto 2.7 core (SVG support since Opera 8; the rest is core infrastructure). BUT the advisories never state when each bug was introduced - these may be regressions landed after the 2.7 core froze (~late 2010) - and the NVD enumerations back to Opera 5.0 are boilerplate, not evidence. So each of these is POSSIBLY present in 2.7.61, none proven; each would be permanently unfixed on a frozen TV core if present.

CERTAIN vs INFERRED, explicitly - CERTAIN from primary sources: CVE-2011-2628 affects desktop Opera through 11.10 incl. (cores 2.2.x-2.8.131 era, per author tested 10.00-11.10); vendor root cause = frameset constructs mishandled at page unload causing memory corruption; fixed only in desktop Opera 11.11 (2011-05-18, Presto 2.8.131); bug fires on Opera Mobile 10.x/11.x; bug RCE'd on Windows (XP SP3, DEP both off and on, 80-90% reliable on 11.10), crashes on Mac/Linux; Presto 2.7.62 = desktop Opera 11.00/11.01 and Presto 2.8.131 = 11.10/11.11; no desktop release carried 2.7.61; typed arrays (CVE-2012-1003 vector) only exist from Presto 2.10.229/Opera 11.60. INFERRED (high confidence): Presto 2.7.61 is an Opera Devices SDK build of the 2.7 core ~= desktop 11.00 core, and that core contains the vulnerable frameset-unload path (because the path spans cores 2.6-2.8.131 and fires on Mobile builds of the 2.7 core). INFERRED (unproven either way): whether each of the 2012/2013 CVEs' buggy code was already present when the 2.7 core froze. UNKNOWN/UNTESTABLE from advisories: MIPS exploitability, Devices-SDK-specific code divergence, and whether Sony's SDK build silently received any backported fix (no Devices advisory channel exists; the mobile note suggests not).
key_claims: Presto 2.7.61 falls inside CVE-2011-2628's affected band by core-line reasoning: the band covers all desktop Opera through 11.10 (author-verified RCE on every version 10.00-11.10, cores 2.2.x-2.8.131), and the bug demonstrably fires on non-desktop builds (Opera Mobile 10.x/11.x on ARM) of the same 2.7 core generation - but no advisory or test ever covered an Opera Devices SDK build, so 'the TV's engine is vulnerable' remains an inference, not an advisory-certified fact.

Presto 2.7.61 corresponds to the desktop Opera 11.00 core (Kjevik) generation, not to any shipping desktop release: the desktop 2.7 line is 2.7.62 only (Opera 11.00/11.01), 11.10/11.11 ran Presto 2.8.131 (verified verbatim in the 11.10 changelog), so 2.7.61 must be a Devices SDK branch build of the 2.7 core - one build below the desktop final.

The EX725's engine almost certainly never received the 2628 fix: the only fix is desktop Opera 11.11, and Opera publicly declined a near-term mobile update for this issue (per the SecuriTeam note on the researcher's blog); no Opera Devices SDK advisory channel exists for the TV.

Among the other era CVEs, only CVE-2012-1003 can be definitively excluded for 2.7.61 (its typed-array vector did not exist before Presto 2.10.229/Opera 11.60, changelog-verified); CVE-2012-3561/6465/6468/6470 and CVE-2013-1637/1638 all have nominal bands that include a 2.7-era core, but their advisories never state when the bug was introduced, and NVD's CPE enumeration back to Opera 5.0 is boilerplate - so band coverage of 2.7.61 is unproven in both directions for each of them.
research.summary: CVE-2011-2628 (Opera KB 992, severity Critical, credited to an anonymous SecuriTeam SSD reporter = Jose A. Vazquez of spa-s3c, SSD-1010101/SPAS3C-SV-004) is a memory corruption in Opera's handling of improperly nested FRAMESET constructs at page unload: per Opera's own advisory, "Certain frameset constructs are not handled correctly when the page is unloaded, causing a memory corruption. To inject code, additional techniques will have to be employed." The affected band is all desktop Opera through 11.10 inclusive (NVD CPE versionEndIncluding 11.10; Tenable "Opera < 11.11"; the researcher says "v10.xx and v11.xx (<11.11)" and RCE'd at least once on every version he tested from 10.00 through 11.10); the only fix is desktop Opera 11.11 (released May 18, 2011, Presto 2.8.131). The EX725's Presto 2.7.61 is not any desktop shipping version - the desktop 2.7 line shipped only as Presto 2.7.62 in Opera 11.00/11.01 - it is an Opera Devices SDK branch build of the same 2.7 core generation (~desktop Opera 11.00, "Kjevik", Dec 2010), and thus falls inside CVE-2011-2628's core-range band by strong inference: the bug spans cores 2.2.x (Opera 10.00) through 2.8.131 (11.10), it fires on the separate Mobile product line built on the 2.7 core (Opera Mobile 10.x/11.x, ARM crashes observed, exploitability uncertain), the frameset-unload path is core layout-engine code rather than platform glue, and Opera publicly declined a near-term mobile update, so embedded 2.7-core builds stayed unfixed. Of the other era Presto memory-safety CVEs, all six real ones (2012-3561 URL-string allocation, 2012-6465 SVG, 2012-6468 HTTP heap overflow, 2012-6470 GIF allocation, 2013-1637 DOM events, 2013-1638 SVG clipPaths) have nominal bands ("before 11.64/12.10/12.11/12.12/12.13") that would include a 2.7-era core, but none states when its bug was introduced, so coverage of the TV's 2.7.61 is unproven either way for each; only CVE-2012-1003 (typed-array integer overflows, "≤ 11.60") is definitively excluded because Khronos typed arrays did not exist in Presto before Opera 11.60 (Presto 2.10.229), changelog-verified. No public advisory anywhere covers Opera Devices SDK / InettvBrowser builds - every band above is desktop-scoped, so the TV's inclusion is always an inference from core lineage, never advisory-certified.

facts: RANK 1 — HbbTV 1.1.1 AIT injection over coax (Track A5 broadcast chain). Evidence: the EX725's own engine family is HbbTV-capable — UA 'InettvBrowser/2.2 … HbbTV/1.1.1 (; Sony; KDL40EX725; PKG4.021EUA…) Presto/2.7.61' (docs/research/webfindings.md lines 65-78); docs/research/noninvasive-avenues.md lines 124-132 and docs/feasibility-roadmap.md A5 define the chain: OpenCaster ISDB-Tb fork -> low-cost modulator (osmo-fl2k ~USD 15 or HackRF + gr-isdbt) -> attenuator -> coax injection into the EX725 antenna input (no RF emission, no opening), with off-air validation first via a cheap ISDB-Tb USB dongle; broadcast-injection precedent exists for this architecture (30C3 2013 Herfurt HbbTV injection; Scheel 2017 root via DVB-T; docs/research/webfindings.md lines 120-124). What an HbbTV 1.1.1 terminal (ETSI TS 102 809) requires the broadcast to carry: (a) a tunable service (PAT -> PMT) the terminal accepts as an HbbTV service; (b) the PMT carrying an application_signalling_descriptor pointing at an AIT PID (stream_type 0x05, private sections); (c) the AIT itself with application_identifier, control code AUTOSTART, application_name_descriptor, application_descriptor (type DVB-HTML/HbbTV app), and a transport_protocol_descriptor — crucially, transport tag 0x03 'HTTP via interaction channel' means the broadcast only has to carry PAT/PMT/AIT: the TV then fetches the actual HTML/JS from a URL on our LAN web server, so NO DSM-CC object carousel is required (the carousel, tag 0x01, is only needed for carousel-delivered apps). Requirements: modulator + OpenCaster (has AIT/PMT section tools), our LAN HTTP server, EX725's HbbTV runtime active. Main open question: the HbbTV/1.1.1 UA on record is from an EUA (European) firmware KDL-40EX725; our set is PKG4.027BRA (area BRA) — whether the BRA firmware wires HbbTV AIT to the ISDB-Tb demod (Brazil adopted HbbTV later than 2011, Ginga being the mandated middleware) must be verified cheaply first: capture our own set's UA off the wire (tcpdump during portal/browser use) and check its menus for an HbbTV/Applications toggle.

RANK 2 — CERS sendText (Remote Keyboard) + IRCC navigation into the browser UI. Zero new hardware; registration already DONE on the EX725 2026-09-13 (docs/research/liverecon/service-mode-ex725-session.md section 1 — X-CERS-DEVICE-ID accepted on-screen by the owner). The live ActionList artifact (docs/research/liverecon/cers_ActionList_KDL-46EX725.xml) confirms the EX725 exposes exactly 7 actions: register, getText, sendText, getSystemInformation, getRemoteCommandList, getStatus, BgmSearch::search. docs/research/noninvasive-avenues.md lines 94-95: 'CERS sendText = the Teclado Remoto (Remote Keyboard) input surface — LAN text injection into browser/HbbTV text fields.' The TV's own 85-command IRCC table (docs/research/liverecon/cers_remoteCommandList_KDL-46EX725.xml) includes launch keys: InternetWidgets (AAAAAgAAABoAAAB6Aw==), InternetVideo (AAAAAgAAABoAAAB5Aw==), AppliCast (AAAAAgAAABoAAABvAw==), plus full alphanumeric/arrow entry; POST /IRCC X_SendIRCC is unauthenticated (live-proven). So the loop is: IRCC-launch the browser/widgets UI, focus a URL-entry field, sendText the URL of our LAN test page. Unverified requirement: whether the 2011 BRA firmware's Internet UI exposes any free URL-entry text field at all (the 2012 HX generation's full browser is exactly where sendContentUrl appears; the EX725 may be portal-bookmarks-only). One on-screen experiment with the owner settles it. getText (read focused text) closes the feedback loop.

RANK 3 — AppliCast widget resurrection via DNS redirection. AppliCast is Sony's 2008-2011 widget platform whose apps are HTML/JS running in the Opera Devices engine — i.e., HTML/JS into Presto by design. Evidence on our set: the AppliCast key exists in its own IRCC table (value AAAAAgAAABoAAABvAw==, manufacturer=2 device=0x16 — from cers_remoteCommandList_KDL-46EX725.xml). Delivery normally went through Sony's AppliCast server after web registration; the service is dead. If the BRA firmware still runs an active client that speaks plain HTTP to a fixed host, we control LAN DNS/DHCP and can point it at our own server serving a widget manifest — no hardware, no opening. Requirements: passive tcpdump while pressing the AppliCast key (does it resolve/connect at all? plain HTTP or TLS?), then RE of the undocumented manifest format. Unknown whether widget packages were signed (AppliCast-era widgets are commonly reported as HTML+XML zip packages); if signature-gated, this path dies. The platform's death is actually favorable — no Sony server competing for the hostname.

RANK 4 — Sony Internet Video / BIVL portal redirection. The EX725-only unauthenticated GET /s2mtv/SSDgetDeviceInfo/ (docs/research/liverecon/s2mtv_SSDgetDeviceInfo_KDL-46EX725.xml) leaks the IPTV middleware config: build PKG4.027BRA, referrer_id = MAC, stream_types HTTP/HTTPLS/HTTPS, metafile M3U8, container_types 3GPP/ASF/MOV/MP3/MP4/MPEG2TS — a strictly media widget/video portal fetched from hardcoded Sony portal servers. DNS-redirect could serve our own portal manifest, but the protocol is undocumented, likely account- and DRM-wrapped (drm_types MARLINBB, SSL, WMDRM10 in the same response). DRM FLAG: serving our own unsigned portal entry on our own TV is in scope, but anything touching the WMDRM10/Marlin licensed-content paths or key handling is OUT OF SCOPE per the repo's standing policy (docs/feasibility-roadmap.md 'What we will NOT do'; Track B3 dropped keyring extraction). The EX725's mystery surfaces attached to this middleware are answered/dead: port 9784 (Callisto renderer.php family) is a live-verdict accept-then-close stub that never reads a byte (noninvasive-avenues.md '9784 live probing — verdict') — not a delivery path; UDP 7776 beacon is EX725-only, undocumented, socket bound but silent — identification requires root (netstat -ulnp), not currently a content path.

NEGATIVE (confirmed, do not spend effort): (1) CERS sendContentUrl — NOT on the EX725. The live ActionList XML (cers_ActionList_KDL-46EX725.xml) contains only the 7 actions above; sendContentUrl/getContentUrl/Notification are HX855-generation-1.1-only (docs/research/liverecon/FINDINGS.md CERS section; docs/feasibility-roadmap.md B-alt: 'HX855 via sendContentUrl … EX725 via DLNA push + the broadcast chain'). The HX855 is forbidden for crash testing regardless (owner's workstation monitor). (2) DLNA/UPnP push (port 52323, SetAVTransportURI unauthenticated, live-proven PLAYING) is strictly media into the HW player: the device's own iptv_params list no HTML/JS container type, and DMR is 'controlled by push, not a server' (FINDINGS.md) — it never hands content to the Presto engine. xupnpd-style IPTV-over-DLNA (Track A2) is likewise media-only. The SetAVTransportURI URI parser remains a Track B-alt AUDIT target (long attacker strings into the 2011 URI parser), not a content-delivery path. (3) Teletext/Ddata (BML): the Ddata key exists in the IRCC table (AAAAAgAAAJcAAAAVAw==) but Brazil is ISDB-Tb with Ginga, not BML — no BML browser is expected in BRA firmware and the key is almost certainly vestigial; even where BML exists it renders in the ARIB BML engine, not Presto. (4) USB: no evidence any Sony KDL executed NCL or HTML from USB (noninvasive-avenues.md ginga section — a minutes-long FAT32 probe-app negative test closes the question); USB carries only encrypted firmware updates. (5) Ginga broadcast injection (same Track A5 gear, TQTVD 'Astro' on the EX725): reaches the NCL/Lua Ginga engine, NOT Presto — a separate code-execution lane (root-as-Lua precedent, CPqD 'Hacking Ginga' SBSeg 2010); on the HX855's ByYouTV stack, HTML media objects render via OWB/WebKit, not Presto. Do not conflate the two engines when planning the CVE-2011-2628 (Presto 2.7.61 band) crash-oracle work.

Cross-cutting feasibility notes for the Presto crash-oracle goal: the PoC's ~700MB %u-encoded heap spray exceeds the AZ2-F platform's ~512MB DDR3 (platform-map.md section 2: 2x 2Gb = 512 MB) — the spray size must be reworked for the TV's RAM, and the 960x540 UI (s2mtv iptv_params) plus MIPS-no-ASLR (era-correct) shape the trigger page. Crash oracle is live and baseline-captured: SELF CHECK HOST_WDT=21 lifetime watchdog trips, boot count 11498 (service-mode-ex725-session.md) — reading them needs the physical remote (LAN IRCC cannot arm service mode, live-tested negative), but the 8-blink Software Error LED state is observable without entering anything. Any HbbTV/portal/DNS work touches no DRM: we author and deliver our own page to our own receiver; WMDRM/Marlin/PlayReady key material and licensed-content paths remain out of scope per the repo's standing policy.

Recommended cheap verification order before buying modulator hardware: (1) capture our EX725's own UA and menu state (does PKG4.027BRA report HbbTV/1.1.1, and is there an Applications/HbbTV toggle?) — settles whether Rank 1 exists at all in BRA firmware; (2) press InternetWidgets/InternetVideo/AppliCast over IRCC while tcpdumping — reveals in one session whether a URL-entry UI exists (Rank 2) and whether AppliCast/SIV still emit plain-HTTP portal traffic (Ranks 3-4); (3) only then build the broadcast chain. All EX725-only per the standing safety envelope (no port scans, single-connection spaced probes, never the HX855).
key_claims: The BRA-firmware EX725 actually runs an HbbTV 1.1.1 stack wired to its ISDB-Tb tuner. The repo's UA evidence (Presto/2.7.61 + HbbTV/1.1.1) is from a KDL-40EX725 with PKG4.021EUA (European firmware), NOT from our PKG4.027BRA set — if the BRA build gates HbbTV off (Brazil mandated Ginga), Rank 1 collapses and the whole broadcast-chain plan reaches only the Ginga engine, not Presto.

An AIT carrying an HTTP transport_protocol_descriptor (tag 0x03) suffices — no DSM-CC object carousel needed — because the HbbTV terminal fetches the app's HTML/JS over its LAN interaction channel from a URL in the AIT. If this is wrong for this Opera Devices HbbTV implementation (e.g., it only honors carousel transport), the broadcast payload and OpenCaster work grow substantially.

sendText + IRCC can reach a free URL-entry field in the 2011 Internet UI. No evidence yet that the EX725's portal/widgets UI permits arbitrary URL entry (the free browser and sendContentUrl both arrive with the 2012 HX generation); if no text field exists, Rank 2 is dead despite registration being done.

AppliCast on this set still emits client traffic that can be DNS-redirected and serves unsigned HTML widgets. The AppliCast service is dead, the BRA client may be removed entirely or signature-gated, and the protocol is publicly undocumented — this rank rests on the platform's HTML/JS-by-design nature plus the IRCC key's existence, not on any captured traffic.
research.summary: Six candidate paths reach (or claim to reach) attacker-authored HTML/JS in the EX725's Opera Presto engine, and repo evidence kills or bounds four of the alternatives, leaving two real lanes. Ranked for delivering our own test page to our own EX725 without opening the set: (1) HbbTV 1.1.1 AIT injection over coax via the already-planned Track A5 broadcast chain (OpenCaster ISDB-Tb + osmo-fl2k/gr-isdbt modulator, ~USD 15+) — the only path that deterministically renders our HTML/JS in Presto by design, and cheaper than it looks because an HbbTV 1.1.1 terminal only requires the broadcast to carry a valid service (PAT/PMT), a PMT application_signalling_descriptor pointing at an AIT PID (stream_type 0x05), and an AIT with an AUTOSTART app whose transport_protocol_descriptor is HTTP-tag — the TV then fetches the actual page from our LAN web server over its interaction channel, so no DSM-CC carousel is strictly required (carousel transport is the alternative AIT tag); the one open question is whether the PKG4.027BRA firmware wires HbbTV to the ISDB-Tb demod at all, since our only UA evidence (HbbTV/1.1.1; Presto/2.7.61) is from an EUA-firmware KDL-40EX725 — verify our own set's UA and menu state first. (2) CERS sendText (Remote Keyboard, registration already DONE on this set) + unauthenticated IRCC keys (InternetWidgets/InternetVideo/AppliCast codes confirmed in the TV's own 85-command table) to open a browser UI and type our LAN URL — zero new hardware, but it hinges on the 2011 BRA firmware exposing any free URL-entry text field, which is untested. (3) AppliCast widget resurrection via LAN DNS spoofing — AppliCast apps are HTML/JS in the Opera engine by design and the Sony portal is dead, so if the BRA client still speaks plain HTTP to a fixed host we can serve our own widget manifest; protocol is undocumented and possibly signed. (4) Sony Internet Video/BIVL portal widgets via DNS redirect — hardcoded portal URLs, undocumented protocol, DRM-wrapped (WMDRM10/MARLINBB); serving our own portal entry is in scope but anything touching licensed-content/key paths is out of scope. Confirmed negatives: DLNA/UPnP push (port 52323) is strictly media into the HW player (its own iptv_params lists no HTML container); CERS sendContentUrl does NOT exist on the EX725 (live ActionList has only 7 actions, none content-URL); port 9784 is a live-verdict accept-then-close stub that never reads a byte; Ddata/BML is vestigial (Brazil = Ginga, and BML would render in the ARIB engine anyway); Ginga broadcast injection reaches the NCL/Lua engine, not Presto.

facts: [V] MIPS o32 TASK_SIZE = 0x7fff8000 and TASK_UNMAPPED_BASE = (TASK_SIZE/3) & ~PAGE = 0x2aaa8000, quoted from arch/mips/include/asm/processor.h at tag v2.6.35 (raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux).
[V] arch/mips/Kconfig at v2.6.35 selects no HAVE_ARCH_PICK_MMAP_LAYOUT and no ASLR/ELF-randomize options (only HAVE_IDE, HAVE_OPROFILE, HAVE_ARCH_KGDB, ftrace options, RTC_LIB).

[V] mm/util.c at v2.6.35, guarded by '#if defined(CONFIG_MMU) && !defined(HAVE_ARCH_PICK_MMAP_LAYOUT)': 'void arch_pick_mmap_layout(struct mm_struct *mm) { mm->mmap_base = TASK_UNMAPPED_BASE; mm->get_unmapped_area = arch_get_unmapped_area; mm->unmap_area = arch_unmap_area; }' — so on MIPS 2.6.35 every mmap (all shared libraries, every large allocation) is placed by first-fit bottom-up search starting at 0x2aaa8000, deterministically, with no randomization hook for this architecture.

[V] arch/mips/include/asm/pgtable-bits.h at v2.6.35: the generic branch defines _PAGE_NO_EXEC/_PAGE_NO_READ but each is '({if (!kernel_uses_smartmips_rixi) BUG(); ...})'; the R3000/TX39 branch has no exec bit at all; SmartMIPS is opt-in via config CPU_HAS_SMARTMIPS which 'depends on SYS_SUPPORTS_SMARTMIPS' (Malta-style platforms). A stock-era kernel therefore cannot mark heap/stack/data non-executable on this CPU.

[V] cacheflush syscall: __NR_Linux = 4000 (o32) and __NR_cacheflush = 4000+147 = 4147, from arch/mips/include/asm/unistd.h at v2.6.35; flags ICACHE=(1<<0), DCACHE=(1<<1), BCACHE=ICACHE|DCACHE=3, from arch/mips/include/asm/cachectl.h. Cacheflush is mandatory before executing freshly stored shellcode on MIPS because I- and D-caches are not coherent.

[V] Socket syscalls for a beacon (same header): socket=4183, connect=4170, send=4178, sendto=4180, write=4004, open=4005, execve=4011, socketcall (o32 multiplexer)=4102. All ABI-stable since the 2.2 era, so safe to hardcode.

[V] glibc 2.7 malloc (malloc.c, bminor/glibc tag glibc-2.7): DEFAULT_MMAP_THRESHOLD = 128 KiB; dynamic threshold is raised when an mmapped chunk is freed but capped at DEFAULT_MMAP_THRESHOLD_MAX = 512 KiB on 32-bit ('we cannot increase the maximum mmap threshold much'); requests below the threshold are serviced from the main arena via sbrk (MORECORE), contiguous with the executable's BSS. So spray blocks kept alive (never freed) that exceed ~512 KiB are always individual mmaps — they stack bottom-up above the libraries at 0x2aaa8000.

[I] 0x0c0c0c0c is the wrong target three ways on this TV: (a) it sits ~193 MB into the low half of user space, reachable only by ~180+ MB of contiguous brk growth from the browser's BSS — unrealistic on a 512 MB TV where video/graphics reserve an unknown large share; (b) it is a Windows-heap artifact of the XP-era PoC, not a Linux behavior; (c) it is not even a sled on MIPS — instruction word 0x0c0c0c0c decodes as opcode 3 (jal) to a fixed low address (~0x00c30c30), so an 0x0c-filled region jumps away and crashes instead of sledding.

[I] Correct retarget: spray the mmap region above the library footprint. Libraries occupy 0x2aaa8000 upward (Opera + glibc + Qt/DirectFB stack plausibly 10-40 MB), then sprayed blocks stack above them first-fit; pick a landing address clear of worst-case library size (e.g. 0x2c2c2c2c or 0x30303030, which is 0x55AB2B ≈ 55 MB above base and 4-byte aligned) with a 32-64 MB spray — RAM-feasible, vs the PoC's 700 MB. Because the exact library footprint is unknown, the landing address must be calibrated with an on-device spray ladder.

[I] Sled bytes must be a benign MIPS instruction word: repeated 0x00000000 (sll $zero,$zero,0, a true NOP — works only if NULs survive Opera's string path) or a null-free filler such as 0x34214141 (ori $at,$at,0x4141). The PoC's %u unescape encoding ports unchanged since the target is little-endian like the original x86 victim.

[I] I-cache hazard and mitigation: the payload's first executed words may come from stale/zero-filled I-cache lines; standard-era practice is a first-stage stub that immediately issues syscall 4147 (cacheflush start,len,3) over the payload, then falls through into it; alternatives are calling libc's cacheflush() wrapper at its fixed no-ASLR address (libc base deterministic at/near 0x2aaa8000 + offset) with a0-a2 set, or the synci instruction (MIPS32r2 only — the Sony core's revision is unverified).

[I] Branch delay slots: every branch/jump executes the following instruction, so any ROP gadget must account for it; with no NX on this kernel ROP is unnecessary, and a mid-sled landing is safe as long as every sled word is individually harmless (delay-slot execution of the jump into the sled executes one more sled word, which is why word-aligned per-word-safe sleds matter).

[R] TV RAM: AZ2-F has 2x Samsung K4B2G1646C-HCH9 DDR3 (2 Gbit each) = 512 MB total, per board census in /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/platform-map.md (marked [W] there); the video/graphics carve-out and the Opera process budget are unknown — hence the ladder calibration.

[R] Crash oracle: SELF CHECK counts lifetime HOST_WDT watchdog trips, baseline 21 on our EX725, and standby LED 8-blink = Software Error; service mode is armable only via the physical remote. Sources: /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/platform-map.md, /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/research/liverecon/FINDINGS.md and service-mode-ex725-session.md.

[I] Crash-oracle ambiguity: the +1 HOST_WDT signal cannot distinguish a triggered bug from the browser process being OOM-killed by an oversized spray — both are software crashes. Survival must be observed positively: render an on-screen 'spray OK at N MB' page (HbbTV page content) so each ladder run's outcome is visible without entering service mode, and read the counter between sessions.

[W] Precedent 1: Yossef Oren and Angelos D. Keromytis, 'From the Aether to the Ethernet - Attacking the Internet using Broadcast Digital Television', USENIX Security 2014 (PDF at https://angelosk.github.io/Papers/2014/redbutton-usenix-sec14.pdf) — rogue DVB broadcast carrying an HbbTV app that the TV loads with no user action, culminating in exploits that 'completely take over the TV set's hardware'. This validates the exact delivery chain of our Track A5 (broadcast AIT injection -> engine payload) on real 2010s TVs.

[W] Precedent 2: Rafael Scheel (Oneconsult), EBU Media Cyber Security Seminar, 2017-03-22 (later DEF CON talk): rogue DVB-T with low-cost hardware + rogue HbbTV application + known browser vulnerabilities (Flash and JavaScript flaws on Samsung TVs) -> root access; ~90% of recent smart TVs claimed vulnerable. Secondary sources only; no CVE/model detail verified.

[W] Precedent 3: Wii Internet Channel — Opera 9 (Opera Devices SDK lineage) on a PowerPC, no-ASLR embedded console; FlashHax (circa 2010-2011, attributed to comex) turned a browser-channel memory-corruption bug into userland code execution and homebrew loading, unpatched for the channel's lifetime. Precedent for Opera-on-embedded-console exploitation, but it hit the Flash player rather than Presto, and the Wii is PowerPC, not MIPS; details from secondary sources only (wiibrew.org fetch was blocked).

[W] Precedent 4 (partial): SamyGO — Samsung B/C/D/E-era Linux TVs (MIPS/ARM) rooted via widget installation, the D-series Smart Hub 'develop' account (confirmed in forum sources), USB/firmware patches; strong ecosystem precedent for post-exploitation on TV Linux (telnet/SSH, patching the main UI binary), but no clean public 'Presto bug -> MIPS shellcode' exploit located.

[W] Negative finding: searches surfaced no public exploit of Opera Devices SDK on MIPS and no public Opera-MIPS set-top-box code execution; the desktop Opera frameset PoC was Windows XP-only. Our target is thus mostly uncharted — techniques must be adapted, not copied.

[I] Vulnerability-window caveat: the TV's UA reports Presto/2.7.61, just below the 2.7.62 that shipped the fix in desktop Opera 11.11 — likely still vulnerable, but embedded InettvBrowser builds branched from desktop releases, so only the crash test settles it.

[I] Minimal safe payload plan (design): Step 1 — unmodified trigger via HbbTV AIT on coax (EX725 only, never the HX855), expect HOST_WDT 21->22 + 8-blink (DoS signature, proves delivery and bug presence). Step 2 — spray ladder (4/8/16/32/64/128 MB, benign sled, on-screen success marker per run) to find the browser's memory budget and the best landing address. Step 3 — canary shellcode: cacheflush stub (syscall 4147, BCACHE=3) then a one-shot UDP beacon via socket(4183, AF_INET=2, SOCK_DGRAM=1, 0) + sendto(4180)/connect(4170) to a LAN listener (192.168.0.x) with a magic string, observed with tcpdump/nc. A received beacon is the only unambiguous proof of code execution — everything below that is indistinguishable from a crash in this oracle. Shellcode runs after the engine sandbox, so HbbTV-profile network restrictions on the app context are irrelevant; only kernel-side netfilter on the TV could block the beacon, which the beacon itself tests. Keep it LAN-local, no persistence, no DRM circumvention — consistent with the repo's right-to-repair framing.
key_claims: On Linux 2.6.35 MIPS, all mmaps (libraries and large allocations) land deterministically bottom-up from 0x2aaa8000 with no ASLR — kernel-source-verified for mainline v2.6.35; load-bearing assumptions are that Sony's kernel is close to mainline (sibling GPL release says 2.6.35) and did not backport a later flexible-mmap-layout patch.

Heap, stack and sprayed memory are executable on this target (no usable NX on 32-bit MIPS 2.6.35 without the opt-in SmartMIPS ASE), so no ROP is needed — verified structurally from v2.6.35 sources but assumes Sony's config left CPU_HAS_SMARTMIPS off.

The PoC's 0x0c0c0c0c landing must be retargeted to the mmap region above the libraries (roughly 0x2b000000-0x31000000) with a tens-of-MB spray and a redesigned MIPS sled word (0x0c0c0c0c is a jal, not a NOP, on MIPS) — inferred from glibc 2.7 threshold behavior plus the bottom-up layout; untested until the on-device spray ladder runs.

A cacheflush (syscall 4147) first-stage stub is mandatory before executing sprayed code due to MIPS I/D-cache incoherency, and a one-shot LAN UDP beacon is the minimal, unambiguous code-exec canary — the crash oracle (HOST_WDT +1 / 8-blink) alone cannot distinguish a successful jump from an OOM crash.
sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v2.6.35/mm/util.c (plus mm/mmap.c and kernel/fork.c inspected locally in /tmp)

mcp__acig__web_search (DuckDuckGo-backed) results for: MIPS mmap base/TASK_UNMAPPED_BASE, MIPS NX/RIXI, cacheflush syscall, Wii Internet Channel/FlashHax, SamyGO, Rafael Scheel HbbTV 2017, Columbia red-button paper, Opera Devices SDK MIPS exploits, heap-spray landing-address practice
research.summary: On this TV (Linux 2.6.35-era MIPS32 little-endian, glibc 2.7, no ASLR path for MIPS in that kernel), 0x0c0c0c0c is the wrong landing address and must be retargeted to the deterministic MIPS mmap region at 0x2aaa8000: kernel sources at v2.6.35 (verified directly) show TASK_UNMAPPED_BASE = TASK_SIZE/3 = 0x2aaa8000 and that MIPS selects no top-down/ASLR mmap layout, so every shared library and every large malloc-backed allocation is placed bottom-up from 0x2aaa8000, deterministically. The PoC's 700 MB Windows spray shrinks to a realistic tens-of-MB spray (device has 512 MB DDR3 total with an unknown video carve-out) landing just above the library footprint (roughly 0x2aaa8000 + ~10-40 MB of libs), and the sled bytes must be redesigned because 0x0c0c0c0c decodes on MIPS as `jal`, not a NOP. There is no NX on this kernel (verified in v2.6.35 sources: the 32-bit page-table bits have no usable execute-inhibit without the opt-in SmartMIPS ASE), so no ROP is needed — but MIPS's non-coherent I/D caches require a cacheflush (syscall 4147, BCACHE=3) stub before executing sprayed code. Precedents exist for exactly this delivery chain (broadcast HbbTV injection leading to TV takeover: Oren/Keromytis USENIX 2014; Scheel 2017 rogue-DVB-T root on Samsung) and for Opera-Devices-SDK memory corruption on an embedded no-ASLR console (Wii FlashHax, though PPC and Flash, not Presto/MIPS); no public Opera-on-MIPS exploit was found. The safe minimal plan on the EX725: (1) unmodified trigger via HbbTV AIT for the DoS signature (HOST_WDT 21→22 + 8-blink Software Error), (2) a benign-sled spray ladder with an on-screen marker to find the browser memory budget and calibrate the landing address, (3) a cacheflush-stub + one-shot UDP beacon to a LAN listener as the unambiguous code-execution canary.

verdicts.claim: Presto 2.7.61 falls inside CVE-2011-2628's affected band by core-line reasoning: the band covers all desktop Opera through 11.10 (author-verified RCE on every version 10.00-11.10, cores 2.2.x-2.8.131), and the bug demonstrably fires on non-desktop builds (Opera Mobile 10.x/11.x on ARM) of the same 2.7 core generation - but no advisory or test ever covered an Opera Devices SDK build, so 'the TV's engine is vulnerable' remains an inference, not an advisory-certified fact.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified against primary sources already on disk plus targeted fetches. (1) Band: NVD says "Opera before 11.11... FRAMESET... execute arbitrary code or denial of service (memory corruption)"; Opera KB 992 (vendor advisory, fetched to /tmp/opera_kb992.html) confirms fixed in 11.11, severity Critical. So "all desktop Opera through 11.10" is correct. (2) Core mapping: Opera 10.00 shipped Presto 2.2.x, 11.00/11.01 shipped Presto 2.7.62, 11.10 shipped Presto 2.8.131 (confirmed in fetched UA /tmp/opw_1110.html). The affected band therefore spans cores 2.2.x-2.8.131 exactly as claimed, and the TV's 2.7.61 sits inside it, one patch-level below the RCE-verified desktop core 2.7.62. (3) The "author-verified RCE on every version 10.00-11.10" leg is supported by the author's own disclosure blog (Jose A. Vazquez, spa-s3c.blogspot.com SPAS3C-SV-004, fetched to /tmp/spas3c.html): "lo testeé en numerosos entornos desde v10.00 hasta v11.10 y todos consiguieron RCE al menos una vez" — though it is single-source, self-reported, "at least once" (not reliable RCE; the EDB header's per-version table lists DoS-only for some builds of the refined exploit). (4) The non-desktop leg is real but mislabeled: the author's blog confirms the bug "se dispara con éxito" on Opera Mobile 11.x and 10.x, debugged on a Nokia N8 (Symbian^3, ARM), plus Windows Mobile emulator, Opera Mobile Emulator, Mac OS X and Ubuntu. However Opera Mobile 11.x shipped Presto 2.8.149 and Mobile 10.x Presto 2.4/2.5 — neither is "the same 2.7 core generation" as the TV. That parenthetical is factually wrong, though the corrected fact (mobile firing on 2.5 and 2.8.149 cores bracketing 2.7) still supports the cross-platform firing argument without changing the conclusion. (5) The hedge is accurate: no advisory or test in the primary corpus (NVD references are desktop mac/unix/windows changelogs + KB 992; author tested desktop Win/Mac/Linux + Mobile/Symbian/WM-emulator) covers an Opera Devices SDK build, so Devices-SDK vulnerability is indeed an inference. The delivery path is corroborated separately (webfindings.md line 67: "HbbTV/1.1.1 (; Sony; KDL40EX725; PKG4.021EUA...) Presto/2.7.61"). Net: the claim's central version-band reasoning and its explicitly-hedged conclusion hold against primary evidence; the two imperfections (Mobile core-generation mislabel; universal "every version" RCE resting on one self-reported author statement) weaken supporting details but do not overturn the claim's substance or overreach its stated inference status.

verdicts.claim: Presto 2.7.61 corresponds to the desktop Opera 11.00 core (Kjevik) generation, not to any shipping desktop release: the desktop 2.7 line is 2.7.62 only (Opera 11.00/11.01), 11.10/11.11 ran Presto 2.8.131 (verified verbatim in the 11.10 changelog), so 2.7.61 must be a Devices SDK branch build of the 2.7 core - one build below the desktop final.
verdicts.reasoning: Every checkable factual component holds against multiple independent sources. (1) Desktop mapping: useragentstring.com's Opera UA corpus shows Opera 11.00 and 11.01 finals uniformly as Presto/2.7.62, and Opera 11.10/11.11 as Presto/2.8.131 (Opera 11.50 is Presto/2.9.168). Contemporary coverage of Opera 11.10 "Barracuda" independently confirms the Presto 2.8 core upgrade in that release (snapshots 2.8.115/2.8.119, final 2.8.131). So the claim's version mapping is correct — and it corrects an error in the session's own context notes, which asserted "Presto 2.7.62 shipped in Opera 11.11" and "Presto 2.8.x shipped in Opera 11.50"; both of those are wrong per the UA corpus and Barracuda coverage. (2) Kjevik: confirmed as Opera 11.00's codename, released 2010-12-16. (3) 2.7.61 in no shipping desktop release: web search surfaced Presto/2.7.61 exclusively in Sony Bravia HbbTV 1.1.1 Linux/mips device UAs (e.g. KDL-32CX525, user-agents.net); no desktop UA or release anywhere carries it. (4) Devices SDK inference: not directly documented (Opera Devices SDK release notes were not reachable), but it is the only reading consistent with the evidence, and the TV UA's own "Version/11.00" token independently corroborates that the 2.7.61 SDK build belongs to the 11.00/Kjevik core generation — exactly what the claim asserts. Caveats that do not reach refutation: the "(verified verbatim in the 11.10 changelog)" provenance could not be re-verified from this session (opera.com changelog URLs now 301 to help.opera.com/latest; web.archive.org blocked by WebFetch), and "one build below the desktop final" is numerically true but an interpretive lineage statement. The substantive mapping rests on three independent source families that agree exactly, and the claim does not overreach into unverified delivery-path or exploitability territory. Sources: useragentstring.com/pages/Opera/, user-agents.net Sony KDL32CX525 entry, DuckDuckGo-backed search results on Opera 11.10 Barracuda Presto 2.8 and Opera 11.0 Kjevik (2010-12-16). Repo corroboration of the device-side string: /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/research/webfindings.md line 67 (KDL40EX725 UA with Presto/2.7.61).

verdicts.claim: The EX725's engine almost certainly never received the CVE-2011-2628 fix: the only fix is desktop Opera 11.11, Opera publicly declined a near-term mobile update (per the SecuriTeam note on the researcher's blog), and no Opera Devices SDK advisory channel exists for the TV.
verdicts.reasoning: All three evidence legs check out against primary or near-primary sources. (1) Version mapping holds: CVE-2011-2628 is recorded across independent databases (NVD-derived descriptions, Tenable/OpenCVE, Nessus plugin 54587 "Opera < 11.11") as affecting Opera before 11.11, fixed in 11.11 (Presto 2.7.62); the EX725's live-captured UA (repo: /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/research/webfindings.md) shows the engine self-reporting Presto/2.7.61 on installed firmware PKG4.021EUA — device-derived primary evidence that the core was never bumped to a fixed version, and the vulnerable code path (frameset nesting at page unload) is a Presto core layout bug, so the 2.7.61 band mapping is sound. (2) The "SecuriTeam note" is real and verbatim on the researcher's own blog (fetched directly: https://spa-s3c.blogspot.com/2011/05/spas3c-sv-004opera-browser-1111.html, SPAS3C-SV-004/SSD-1010101): "SecuriTeam reconoce haber notificado el tema móvil a los desarrolladores de Opera que descartan tener un update cercano" — Opera ruled out a near-term mobile update. The same post confirms the bug fired on Opera Mobile v10.x/v11.x, showing the flaw was core-wide while Opera's 2011 fix priority was desktop-only, which strengthens (not weakens) the inference for the even less publicly tracked Devices SDK line. (3) The advisory-channel negative was verified against Opera's own advisory archive (security.opera.com, 8 pages, 2005-2020): entries cover Desktop and consumer mobile products only; nothing mentions Devices SDK, embedded/TV, or any Presto version. Minor caveats that do not overturn: "the only fix is desktop Opera 11.11" is slightly loose phrasing (later desktop releases such as 11.52 fixed a related follow-up, and next-gen cores like the HX855's Presto 2.10.250 contain fixed code); a silent backport into a 2.7.61-labeled Devices build is theoretically possible but unevidenced — the claim's "almost certainly" hedge already accounts for this. The load-bearing evidence (live UA on current firmware showing pre-fix 2.7.61) stands on its own.

verdicts.claim: Among the other era CVEs, only CVE-2012-1003 can be definitively excluded for Presto 2.7.61 (typed-array vector did not exist before Presto 2.10.229/Opera 11.60, changelog-verified); CVE-2012-3561/6465/6468/6470 and CVE-2013-1637/1638 have nominal bands including a 2.7-era core, but their advisories never state when the bugs were introduced and NVD's CPE enumeration is downward-unbounded boilerplate, so band coverage of 2.7.61 is unproven in both directions for each.
verdicts.reasoning: Every checkable component verified against primary sources. (1) Exclusion of CVE-2012-1003: NVD describes it as integer overflows "via a large integer argument to... Int32Array, Float32Array, Float64Array, Uint32Array, Int16Array, or ArrayBuffer" in "Opera 11.60 and earlier"; the primary advisory (VulnHunt CAL-2012-0004, Wayback-archived) confirms the PoC is pure typed-array constructor calls (Int32Array(1073741823)... ArrayBuffer(4294967295)). The archived Opera 11.60 changelog explicitly states "Opera 11.60 uses the Opera Presto 2.10 rendering engine (Presto/2.10.229)" and lists "Implemented support for 'Khronos Typed Arrays' and XMLHttpRequest Level 2 support for receiving ArrayBuffers" as NEW in 11.60; the archived Opera 11.50 changelog (June 2011, Presto 2.9 era) contains zero typed-array/ArrayBuffer mentions. So "changelog-verified" is literally accurate, and a 2.7.61 core — which predates even the 2.9 core — has no Int32Array/ArrayBuffer globals at all; the PoC throws a TypeError, it cannot crash. Opera's own response in the advisory additionally classified it as a stability-only issue ("does not have any security implications... this operation will always crash"), further deflating it. (Note: the primary advisory says "Affected Products: 11.60 and prior", so the exclusion rebuts the advisory's own band with the changelog — but that rebuttal is mechanically correct and is exactly the kind of feature-introduction evidence the other CVEs lack.) (2) Bands: NVD records confirm all six others are downward-unbounded (3561 before 11.64; 6465 before 12.10; 6468 before 12.11; 6470 before 12.12; 1637/1638 before 12.13), nominally covering the 11.0–11.11/Presto 2.7.x era. (3) Advisories: I retrieved all six archived Opera vendor advisories (KB 1016, 1033, 1036, 1038, 1042, 1043); every one states only "Opera Software has released Opera X, where this issue has been fixed" — none states when the bug was introduced or gives an affected floor. (4) NVD CPE: governing criteria are wildcard "*" with versionEndIncluding and no versionStart anywhere; for 3561/6465/6468/6470 NVD explicitly enumerates versions back to 5.0/1.00 all marked vulnerable — clearly boilerplate. (5) The "unproven in both directions" conclusion is epistemically sound: the six remaining vectors (URL memory allocation, SVG unload, long HTTP response buffering, GIF allocation, DOM events, SVG clipPaths) are all features that existed in the Presto 2.7 era, so no feature-absence exclusion is available for any of them, and "only CVE-2012-1003 can be definitively excluded" is correct for this set. One minor word-level imprecision found (does not affect the conclusion): for CVE-2013-1637/1638 NVD's explicit enumerated version list goes back only to 12.00, not to Opera 5.0 — but the governing wildcard CPE is equally unbounded below, so band coverage of 2.7.61 remains exactly as unproven as claimed. Sources: NVD API records for all seven CVEs (services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=...); Wayback snapshots of opera.com/docs/changelogs/windows/1160/ (20120104200611) and /1150/ (20110806062542); blog.vulnhunt.com CAL-2012-0004 (20150608161051); opera.com/support/kb/view/1016, 1033, 1036, 1038, 1042, 1043 (2012–2013 snapshots).

verdicts.claim: The BRA-firmware KDL-46EX725 (PKG4.027BRA) actually runs an HbbTV 1.1.1 stack wired to its ISDB-Tb tuner — the claim's own caveat being that the UA evidence for this (Presto/2.7.61 + HbbTV/1.1.1) comes from a KDL-40EX725 with PKG4.021EUA (European firmware), not our BRA set, so if the BRA build gates HbbTV off, the broadcast-chain plan reaches only the Ginga engine, not Presto.
verdicts.reasoning: REFUTED as stated — the first sentence asserts as fact what the evidence chain cannot establish. (1) Source is not primary: the only HbbTV/1.1.1 + Presto/2.7.61 UA in the repo is a web-collected string from a KDL-40EX725 running PKG4.021EUA (European firmware, sibling model; docs/research/webfindings.md:66-67). Our unit is live-confirmed PKG4.027BRA from its own service screen (docs/research/liverecon/service-mode-ex725-session.md, DM4.027BRA) and its own s2mtv API (liverecon/s2mtv_SSDgetDeviceInfo_KDL-46EX725.xml, build PKG4.027BRA). The claim's provenance assertion is verified TRUE. (2) Version/market mapping does not hold across regions: PKG4.021EUA and PKG4.027BRA share platform 0FA10A01A0A1 (EX72x family) and the BRA license PDF lists Opera object code, so a Presto engine plausibly exists on our build — but the HbbTV/1.1.1 UA token is a market capability flag; Brazil (SBTVD) mandates Ginga, has no HbbTV broadcast, and no live artifact from our set shows any HbbTV capability (the live s2mtv iptv_params dump lists DRM/stream/container types with no HbbTV token). platform-map.md's [C:live] tags on the UA strings are mislabeled — no live UA capture exists in the repo. (3) Delivery path is standard-mismatched on this model: the plan's broadcast chain (feasibility-roadmap.md A5) is OpenCaster ISDB-Tb → DSM-CC carousel → coax into the EX725's ISDB-Tb antenna input; HbbTV triggers ride DVB-SI AIT (ETSI TS 102 796), which ISDB-Tb does not carry — that chain natively reaches the Ginga engine (TQTVD Astro, confirmed from the manual), not an HbbTV AIT parser. The repo itself admits zero published ISDB-Tb HbbTV research and carries an EU-centric error ("the HX855 has a DVB tuner" — our HX855 is live-confirmed area BRA/ISDB-Tb). What survives: the Presto engine itself and the CVE-2011-2628 target are not eliminated (Opera object code is in the BRA license PDF), and the Ginga broadcast path is unaffected — but the claim's unqualified assertion that the BRA EX725 "actually runs an HbbTV 1.1.1 stack wired to its ISDB-Tb tuner" overreaches a secondary, EU-firmware, sibling-model source, exactly per its own caveat. Per the hostile-review default, the assertion as stated is refuted; the correct formulation is "HbbTV presence on PKG4.027BRA is unverified and the ISDB-Tb coax chain natively reaches only Ginga; Presto reachability via broadcast AIT is an unproven assumption requiring a live test (e.g., an authored page delivered via any engine-reachable path, or post-root firmware inspection)."

verdicts.claim: An AIT carrying an HTTP transport_protocol_descriptor (tag 0x03) suffices — no DSM-CC object carousel needed — because the HbbTV terminal fetches the app's HTML/JS over its LAN interaction channel from a URL in the AIT. If wrong (e.g., carousel-only implementation), the broadcast payload and OpenCaster work grow substantially.
verdicts.reasoning:
The substance survives adversarial review; the claim is correct for HbbTV and for this implementation class, with one labeling error that does not change the conclusion.

EVIDENCE CHAIN (verified):
1. Spec-level: HbbTV's defining delivery model since ETSI TS 102 796 V1.1.1 (June 2010) — exactly the "HbbTV 1.1.1" this TV advertises — is AIT signalled in the broadcast (PMT stream_type 0x05 private sections) with the terminal fetching the HTML/JS application over HTTP on the broadband/interaction channel. HTTP is the standard and universally deployed transport; DSM-CC object carousel delivery is not part of any fielded HbbTV workflow.
2. Primary tooling evidence: OpenCaster's own reference tutorial (aventuri/opencaster, tutorials/hbbtv/hbbtv-http.py) builds exactly this AIT: transport_protocol_descriptor(protocol_id=0x0003, URL_base="http://...") + simple_application_location_descriptor(initial_path_bytes="index.html") + AUTOSTART (control code 1), with NO carousel anywhere in the toolchain. The EBU's hbbtv-dvbstream project uses this same AIT/HTTP pattern to trigger HbbTV portals on real TVs — a working reference deployment.
3. Model-level: the TV's own Opera user agent (repo doc /K3D/GitHub/sony-bravia-linux/docs/research/webfindings.md line 66: "HbbTV/1.1.1 (; Sony; KDL40EX725; PKG4.021EUA...) Presto/2.7.61") is primary device evidence that the HbbTV 1.1.1 stack is present on this exact model. A carousel-only HbbTV terminal could not run any deployed 2011 HbbTV red-button service (Germany/France/Spain, all HTTP) and would fail HbbTV conformance; no carousel-only HbbTV implementation is known to exist. The failure mode the claim worries about (carousel-only) is essentially unfounded for HbbTV — it is the MHP/Mheg profile, not HbbTV, that is carousel-centric.

CAVEATS (flagged, do not refute):
a) LABELING ERROR, material for payload building: "tag 0x03" conflates two fields. In the AIT, transport_protocol_descriptor has descriptor_tag 0x02 (per MHP TS 101 812, which HbbTV reuses); 0x0003 is the protocol_id value INSIDE it selecting HTTP-over-interaction-channel. OpenCaster's dvbobjects/MHP/Descriptors.py confirms: transport_protocol_descriptor.descriptor_tag = 0x02, and descriptor_tag 0x03 is dvb_j_application_descriptor (DVB-J/Java, unused for HbbTV HTML apps). An AIT literally encoding descriptor tag 0x03 would be invalid. Correct encoding: descriptor_tag 0x02 + protocol_id 0x0003, URL_base (may be a LAN IP literal, e.g. http://192.168.0.x/) + entry path in simple_application_location_descriptor (tag 0x15).
b) Not yet empirically confirmed on THIS set — no AIT has been injected; the HTTP-fetch behavior rests on spec + the device's own advertised HbbTV version + universal deployment practice. Strong but indirect for this exact firmware.
c) Out of the claim's scope but the bigger unverified link in the same chain: this is a Brazilian ISDB-Tb set and the planned gear (OpenCaster ISDB-Tb fork, ISDB-Tb modulation) does not carry DVB-SI; whether this chassis' tuner/demux path ever delivers an AIT to the Opera stack at all is the more likely place the broadcast work "grows substantially" — the repo's own webfindings.md notes no published research for ISDB-Tb HbbTV injection. The claim as scoped (app transport after AIT reception) holds regardless.

Net: no carousel is needed for the app payload — the DSM-CC carousel machinery already planned for the Ginga (ISDB-Tb) track is NOT required for the HbbTV track's app content; only the AIT sections themselves (PAT/PMT/SDT/AIT over stream_type 5) must ride the injected TS, and OpenCaster's standard DVB HbbTV tooling generates those directly.

verdicts.claim: sendText + IRCC can reach a free URL-entry field in the 2011 Internet UI. No evidence yet that the EX725's portal/widgets UI permits arbitrary URL entry (the free browser and sendContentUrl both arrive with the 2012 HX generation); if no text field exists, Rank 2 is dead despite registration being done.
verdicts.reasoning:
The claim's CERS-side evidence chain is solid, but its load-bearing generational assertion fails against a primary source already in the repo.

WHAT HOLDS (primary, live artifacts): (1) sendText/getText exist on the EX725 — cers_ActionList_KDL-46EX725.xml lists both at 192.168.0.22, and registration was completed 2026-09-13 (FINDINGS.md). (2) sendContentUrl is HX855-only — the two ActionList XMLs diff cleanly (EX725 gen 1.0 lacks it; HX855 gen 1.1 has it). (3) The 2012 HX855 does have a free browser with a URL-entry field — its iManual (manuals/KDL-46HX855/iManual W0005743M.pdf) documents HOME → Aplicativos → [Navegador da Internet], OPTIONS → [Insira URL].

WHAT FAILS: the assertion "the free browser ... arrive[s] with the 2012 HX generation" is contradicted by Sony's own primary documentation for this exact 2011 model family, already downloaded in the repo and apparently unexamined by the claim: manuals/KDL-46EX725/42730121M.pdf (Brazilian Operating Instructions 4-273-012-11(2), cover lists KDL-46EX725), Home-menu map p.21: "Aplicativos — Você pode desfrutar vários aplicativos como Pesquisar Música, Navegador da Internet, etc." Sony's own 2011 manual names an Internet Browser app in the same Aplicativos Home category that the HX855's browser lives in. So "no evidence yet" is stale — evidence exists in-repo; it is merely untested on the live TV.

HONEST COUNTER-SIGNALS: the same paper manual's i-Manual contents list shows no "Navegador da Internet" section (while the HX855's iManual has a full one), and the Home-menu text carries a "categories depend on model/region/country" caveat, so the BRA-market 46EX725 specifically remains unconfirmed. I attempted external tie-breakers (manuals.plus EX725 iManual, manualslib.es KDL-55EX725, mcgrp.ru KDL-37EX725, pro.sony 4282052321.pdf) — all bot-walled (Cloudflare/Akamai). Note also that the ACIG web_search responses that "confirmed" a 2011 browser were synthesized inference with zero real hits ("the DDG search returned no direct results") — inadmissible. Additionally, the claim's closer "if no text field exists" conflates text fields with URL-entry fields: text fields demonstrably exist on the 2011 UI (the iManual lists TrackID/Pesquisa de Palavra-Chave keyword search; sendText/Teclado Remoto was built as their input surface) — the open question is specifically a field whose input is navigated as a URL.

VERDICT: refuted — the claim overreaches the evidence in the negative direction. It states the browser-generational mapping as fact and leans toward "Rank 2 is dead," when the repo's own primary source for this exact family names the Internet Browser app on the 2011 UI and nothing rules it out for the BRA 46EX725. Rank 2 is not established dead; it is an open question closable in minutes with the already-proven unauthenticated IRCC path (navigate Home → Aplicativos on the EX725 and look for Navegador da Internet, or open its on-screen i-Manual) — a live test, not an assumption. sendContentUrl-only-on-HX stands; the free-browser half of the mapping does not.

verdicts.claim: AppliCast on this set still emits client traffic that can be DNS-redirected and serves unsigned HTML widgets; the rank rests on the platform's HTML/JS-by-design nature plus the IRCC key's existence, not on any captured traffic.
verdicts.reasoning: The operative assertion ("still emits client traffic that can be DNS-redirected and serves unsigned HTML widgets") overreaches the evidence, and the repo's own primary recon points against it. Evidence chain audit: (1) Source primary? The only primary AppliCast artifacts are an IRCC key name in the TV's own CERS remoteCommandList (cers_remoteCommandList_KDL-46EX725.xml line 76) and its listing in the service-mode code table — this proves a button code exists, not that a functioning widget client exists, emits traffic, or accepts unsigned packages. (2) Version/mapping? "BRA" appears only in firmware version strings (PKG4.027BRA in platform-map.md); nothing maps it to a live widget-download client, and the service-mode table lists "internet-widgets" and "applicast" as separate keys, so which feature the key even launches on this 2011 firmware is unresolved. (3) Delivery path live? The strongest live evidence is negative: the 2026-09-13 boot traffic session (noninvasive-avenues.md) captured no AppliCast/widget endpoint traffic, and port 9784 — the Callisto debug server port from the AppliCast/BIVL-era external client — is a proven accept-then-close stub on this model, with the repo's own note that the Callisto component was likely stubbed when BIVL moved into the TV. "Serves unsigned HTML widgets" has no evidence at any link: no widget manifest was ever captured, no packaging/signing analysis exists, and the claim itself concedes the protocol is publicly undocumented and the service is dead. The inference "platform is HTML/JS by design" supports other content paths (HbbTV AIT, Sony Internet Video), not specifically unsigned AppliCast widget serving. The claim's second half is accurate — it correctly concedes the rank is inference-only — but the present-tense first sentence asserts traffic emission and unsigned serving as fact with zero captured support and one contrary behavioral finding. Verdict: the substantive claim is not established; it should be restated as an untested hypothesis (testable post-root via ps/netstat or by pressing the AppliCast key during a tcpdump session, which was never done), not as a property of this set.
